title: Science of Reading KISS 2026
author: McKeown, Margaret
source: Making Words Make Sense / Harriett Janetos (harriettjanetos.substack.com), September 9,
summary: Guest author Margaret McKeown, a longtime literacy researcher, argues that the Science of Reading movement is drowning in unnecessary complexity and offers a deliberately compressed, 'KISS' (Keep It Short and Simple) restatement of what the research actually supports. She splits the task into two 100-word statements: one defining the science itself (skilled reading depends on high-quality phonological, orthographic, and semantic word knowledge that enables automatic word identification and meaning access) and one defining the instructional implications (efficient systematic phonics, explicit vocabulary work, and content-focused comprehension instruction built around genuine questions). She then works through common objections — comprehension strategies, syntax instruction, writing-reading connections, independent reading — reframing most of them as processes within her core framework rather than additions to it. The piece's underlying argument is methodological as much as substantive: that clarity itself is a instructional virtue, and that adding more terminology around the Science of Reading risks obscuring rather than strengthening the underlying consensus.
points: Proposes describing the entire Science of Reading in roughly 100 words, and its instructional implications in another 100, as a discipline against jargon creep.
Frames vocabulary knowledge as the linchpin of comprehension, not just one input among many.
Treats common 'add-ons' (comprehension strategies, syntax instruction) as processes already contained within identifying/connecting/integrating word meaning, not separate skills to bolt on.
Insists systematic phonics should be taught 'efficiently, not exhaustively' — simplicity as a design constraint, not a shortcut.
Argues that even top readers benefit from thoughtful, efficient literacy instruction — simplicity isn't just for struggling readers.
quotes: KISS is a design philosophy that says systems work best when they stay simple rather than becoming unnecessarily complex. It has its modern origins in the US Navy, attributed to Kelly Johnson, a lead engineer at Lockheed who designed spy planes.

Skilled reading requires readers to have high-quality lexical knowledge consisting of strong phonological, orthographic, and semantic components of words. Such knowledge allows automatic access to a word's identity - what it looks and sounds like - and its meaning, as a reader encounters it in text.

Vocabulary knowledge is the linchpin of comprehension. Comprehension operates as a reader moves through text, identifying words, figuring out meanings of the words relevant to the context, and integrating the words into the context.

Systematic phonics, taught efficiently not exhaustively, including successive blending, set for variability, and attention to word meaning: knowledge of letter-sound patterns and flexibility in applying them, followed by abundant practice reading words, sentences, and most importantly, text.
I don't think these are strategies, but processes that are part of comprehension – which consist of identifying, connecting, and integrating as one proceeds through a text.
Viewing the Science of Reading as simply the knowledge and processes needed for reading can clarify our understanding and pave the way for a set of effective and efficient instructional approaches.
